title: What is known about 1RB1LB_1LC1LA_1RD0LB_1RA1RE_1RF0RD_---1RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LB_1LC1LA_1RD0LB_1RA1RE_1RF0RD_---1RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and looks hard. The run is a sequence of epochs; each multiplies a counter Y by about 5/2 (Y → 5⌊Y/2⌋ + c, c ∈ {0, 5, 10}) and lets a carry, steered by the parity of Y, rewrite the front of a tail of digits. The machine can halt only if a carry runs through the whole tail. For some parity sequences that happens within ten epochs, so no argument that ignores the parities can work; along the real run the tail has grown to 1,311 digits by epoch 4,000 and no carry has gone deeper than three digits. Lean proves the rounds of an epoch, the epoch itself by induction, and several reset shapes.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 61,750 cells have been visited and 34,521 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The two halves of a round
claims.text: From 0^inf 1 B> 1 01 (1^10)^j 0101 1^5 (01)^Y R the machine reaches the same tape with five more ones and the marker 01 (30j+19 steps), and from there, with two a's fewer and the marker 0101 again, (1^10)^(j+1) (30j+51 steps). For all j, Y and every tape R.

claims.title: An epoch, by induction
claims.text: k rounds take c0 j (Y+2k) R to c0 (j+k) Y R: the counter's a's are turned into ones, ten for every two a's, for any k.

claims.title: Resets, for families of first digits
claims.text: When the counter runs out, a sweep turns the 10(j+1)+5 ones back into 5(j+1)+c a's and rewrites the front digits: (2k+2, e+1) → (2k+3, e) with c = 0; (3, e+3) → (1,4)(1,e+1) with c = 5; (1,1)(1,e+3) → (2,2)(1,e+1) and (1,1)(3,e+3) → (2,7)(1,e+1) with c = 0; for all j, k, e and R.

claims.title: The epoch map, checked against the machine
claims.text: py/epochs.py --check 14 runs the machine itself (exact accelerated simulator py/tsim.py) for 7.3·1011 steps and finds the first 13 epoch starts exactly where the epoch map (rounds skipped by formula, reset simulated) puts them.

claims.title: 4,000 epochs without a halt
claims.text: Iterating the epoch map 4,000 times (Y reaches 1,593 decimal digits) never halts; the tail grows to 1,311 digits, about one digit every three epochs, and the carry changes at most the first three digits.

claims.title: Halting is possible in principle
claims.text: Choosing the parity of Y freely at every epoch (both branches), some choices from the real starting tail make the carry run off the end and halt after 10 epochs (e.g. tail (1,1)(19,0) 1^4). So non-halting would have to use the actual parity sequence.
claims.where: search over both parities, notes in README.md

claims.title: Why it probably never halts
claims.text: With the parity of Y treated as a fair coin, the carry depth has an exponential tail (depth ≥5 a few times in 5,000 epochs) while the tail grows linearly; the chance that a carry ever crosses the 1,311 digits now present is astronomically small. Like Mahler's 3/2 problem, the parities themselves are out of reach.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Equivalent to: does a reset carry ever run through the whole tail of digits (and then read 1 0 0 in state D)?

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and the reason is a number-theory puzzle in disguise. The machine keeps a counter that grows by a factor of about 5/2 each epoch; whether the counter is odd or even decides how a carry ripples into a tail of digits. It halts only if one carry ever runs all the way through that tail.

facts.text: 13 epochs of the real machine match the epoch map.
No halt; counter Y has 1,593 decimal digits, the tail 1,311 digits.
Rounds and epoch proved in Lean for all sizes.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.494). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 61,750 cells (44,912 left of the start, 13 right), with a density of 1s of 0.559.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A block, a counter and a tail of digits
html: Everything happens left of the start. Write a for the pair 01. At the start of an epoch the tape reads
a counter of Y a's, then a tail of digits (d, e) = 1^(5d) a^e ending in the fixed word 1^4 a. From blank tape the first epoch starts at step 494 with Y = 5 and tail (1,8).

sections.heading: Rounds: two a's become ten ones
html: Between the head's left end and the counter sits a block of ones, empty at first. In each round the head runs right through the block (turning it into a's as it goes, 11 → 10), zigzags back over it turning the a's back into ones, and adds five. Every second round two a's of the counter are used up. So after Y/2 pairs of rounds the block holds 5Y ones (5Y+5 if Y was even, after one more half round) and the counter is empty. A round costs about three times the block length, so an epoch costs about 3.75·Y2 steps and the visited tape grows like the square root of the time.
Lean: round_a, round_b (one round, any j, Y) and epoch (any number of rounds, by induction).

sections.heading: The reset: halve, and carry
html: When the counter is empty, one sweep turns the block of 10j+5 ones into a's again: two ones per a, so the new counter is about half the block, Y' = 5⌊Y/2⌋ + c with c ∈ {0, 5, 10}. Then the sweep runs on into the tail. It passes a digit only if its block of ones is odd and it has exactly one a; otherwise it turns back and rewrites the digits it passed and the one it stopped at. Which digits it meets first depends on the parity of Y: for even Y the counter's 1^5 merges with the first digit, for odd Y one digit (1,1) is left in front.

sections.heading: The counter explodes, the tail grows slowly
html: The counter gains about 0.4 decimal digits per epoch (a factor of 5/2). The tail gains a digit about every three epochs, because new digits are made at its front and the carry almost never reaches far: in 4,000 epochs it changed at most the first three digits.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The only halting transition is F reading 0, and F is entered only from D> 1 0; the sweep halts exactly when it meets 1 0 0, i.e. if it passes every digit of the tail and arrives at the right end out of step. That needs a long run of special parities of Y. If we pick the parities ourselves, we can make the machine halt within ten epochs of the real start; the real parities come from Y → 5⌊Y/2⌋ + c, a sequence of the same kind as Mahler's 3/2 problem, about which nothing is known. Treating them as coin flips, the carry reaches depth 5 a few times in 5,000 epochs and the tail is already 1,311 digits long, so a halt is extremely unlikely, but it is not excluded.

family: 5/2 Collatz-like counter feeding a carry chain
summary: Epochs: a counter Y of a's is turned into 5Y ones and back into about 5Y/2 a's; the parity of Y (a Mahler-like 5/2 sequence) drives a carry into a growing tail of digits. Halts only if the carry ever runs to the end of the tail; open.
